CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Archery — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the archery club habit safely: real bows wait for the range and its trained coaches, while at home the aim, the breath and the stillness train first.

What is this?

Archery club is the target sport — draw, aim, hold, release — practiced under trained coaches at a proper range. The card’s printed skills are Aim & Focus: choosing the target and holding body and mind still until the moment. The home version trains everything EXCEPT the arrow.

What does it mean?

Archery is mostly a stillness sport: the shot happens in the pause, and the pause is trainable. Beanbag targets, sock throws and held poses all build the same two muscles — the eye that picks a target and the body that waits.

What does the child need to know?

At home: beanbags, a laundry basket or chalk target, clear space, and patience. At the range: a trained coach (certified), loaner bows sized for children, arm guards, and rules everyone follows before anything flies.

Why this matters

Aim-and-focus training transfers everywhere — throwing, catching, handwriting steadiness, and the emotional habit of one calm breath before any attempt. And the range visit, when it comes, lands on prepared ground: the child already knows how to aim and wait.

What it teaches

Target focus, breath control, stance stability, follow-through habits, and the safety mindset that real equipment deserves real training.

Words to learn

aimtargetfocusdrawholdreleaserangecoachbreath

Say this to your child

“"Archery club trains the aim first — the bows live at the range with the coaches. Home practice: beanbag, breath, freeze... and hold the pose! Focus is a muscle. Ready?"”

Step by step

  1. Home target one: beanbags at a hoop — three steps back, one slow breath, toss, and HOLD the follow-through pose for two seconds.
  2. Home target two: rolled socks at the laundry-basket bullseye — move back one step each round.
  3. The archer stance drill: feet apart, body tall, five-second freeze before every throw — the freeze is the actual archery.
  4. Breath habit: in through the nose, out slow, release ON the exhale — the same timing real archers use.
  5. When the family is ready: book a session at a proper range with a certified coach, and the child arrives already knowing how to aim, breathe and hold.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the archer’s arm guard sits snug against the sleeve and the bow is drawn halfway — real archery wears protection and starts with lessons, which is exactly why the coach comes before the arrows.

Ask your child

"When do we release in archery?" (on the slow exhale) "Why do we hold the pose after the throw?" (follow-through is aim’s last half) "Where do real bows live?" (the range, with trained coaches)

What your child can say or do

Your child may chalk bullseyes on every wall (outdoors, ideally), hold five-second freezes unprompted all week, or ask when the range visit happens — the answer: when the coach says yes.

Out in the real world

Olympic archers, bowhunters and historical reenactors all learned the same order: stance, breath, aim, then equipment. Coaches and ranges keep the sport safe — no exceptions, no shortcuts.

Try it together

Point-ladder tournament: each family member gets three beanbag throws from the same line, points by ring, and the ladder climbs one step back per round. Focus wins; laughter keeps the league alive.

Understanding check

Ask: "What trains before the bow?" (aim, breath, stance) "Who teaches real archery?" (a trained coach at a range) "What happens on the exhale?" (the release)

Staying safe

Ask a grown-up and a trained coach. Real bows and arrows belong at a proper range with certified instruction, safety gear and range rules — home practice trains aim and patience only, and never touches arrows.

This lesson pairs with the Archery flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
